73_marg1169: Who, being the brightness of his glory, etc. Here he commends him according to the divine nature, showing Christ to be coeternal and coequal with the Father and of the same substance with him, but another in person. Note how here he enters upon two ways: the one calling us back from the impious error of Sabellius, the other from the error of Arian impiety; lest the Father be thought either not to have an only-begotten, or the Son to subsist as a stranger to the Father. For there are some who rave that he is a stranger, which was Arius’s wicked view. Others labour to feign not one Father and another Son, but the same at one time Father, at another Son. He therefore warns with a complete account both that he is the Son of God, and that he does not exist as alien from him. But we ought to take this with a religious understanding, and if anything absurd perhaps occurs, to drive it from the eye of the mind. For everywhere we have need of a religious understanding, but most of all where we either say or hear something about God; for neither is the tongue sufficient to speak worthily of God, nor does the understanding avail to perceive. For we understand many things of God which we are utterly unable to speak, and we rightly speak many things which we are not fit to understand. For example: that God is everywhere we know and say, but how he is everywhere we do not grasp by understanding. Likewise: that there is a certain incorporeal power which is the cause of all good things we know, but what it is we utterly do not know. There are also some things which cannot be said, although they are grasped by the mind, so that we see even Paul himself in some such matters as if wavering, and not setting forth complete examples, as here when he says: Who being the brightness, etc. Using improper names, because he could not find proper ones, and the likeness of temporal things to show the truth of eternal things, that is, the coeternity of the Father and the Son, although temporal things cannot be compared with eternal things in a complete comparison. For in eternity there is stability, in time variety; in eternity all things stand, in time some succeed others. In creation we find nothing coeternal, because nothing is eternal, but it suffices for the likeness that we find the coeval. For we call coeval whatever have the same measure of times, nor is the one preceded by the other in time. Yet we say both began to be. Even if we can find coeval things in creation, yet not a begetter and begotten, as in the Trinity, generally, the coeternal only-begotten. For in creatures the begotten does not begin from the moment the begetter does. But in the Creator the begetter did not precede the begotten. Therefore temporal things cannot be compared with eternal in a complete comparison, but yet, by some slight and small likeness, the coeval can be compared with the coeternal. Let us therefore find coeval things. For we are admonished by the Scriptures to these likenesses. For we read it written of wisdom itself: “She is the brightness of eternal light.” Likewise: “and the unspotted mirror of God’s majesty.” Behold, wisdom itself is called the brightness of eternal light, that is, the image of the Father, and a mirror. And here the Apostle says: Brightness of glory. For the Son is coeternal with the Father, as brightness is coeval with fire. For if I wish to light a lamp, there is not yet fire there nor brightness, but as soon as I have lit it, the brightness exists likewise and with the fire. Therefore the Son of God is called the brightness of glory in this respect, that the Father is always his, in that he has one of whom he is; not in the sense that the Father was first and afterwards the Son, for always the Father, always the Son is of the Father. Therefore the Son is always born, the Father is always, and the image always from him. Behold, you could not find coeternal things in creatures and you have found coeval ones, by the proportion of which you understand the Son coeternal with the eternal begetter. For what is coeval with the temporal, this is coeternal with the eternal. But it must be observed that although in these, namely fire and brightness, there is coevality, yet there is not complete equality there, because the brightness which is poured forth there from the fire shines less than the fire itself; so these have a likeness, but not complete equality. Therefore by the proportion of other temporal things, of which one is from the other, though not coeval, yet consubstantial, the Son is shown to be consubstantial with the Father. For man is born of man, and horse of horse. Nor is either of these coeval with the other, because the one born is preceded in time by him of whom he is born; but yet both that man and this man, and that horse and this horse, that is, are of the same substance; they are different in time, but are not different in nature. Likewise God the Son is born of God the Father, and since he is coeternal with him he is also of the same nature, not less than he, because God of God, as man born of man is of the same substance, and horse of horse. Behold another kind of likeness: here equality is praised, there coevality. Join therefore this: that everything praiseworthy in creatures, to which something is lacking, is together in the Creator, to whom nothing is lacking; yet what we find there, that is, man and man are two men, but here Father and Son are one God. Therefore the Apostle says: Who being the brightness of glory. The Father is glory, the Son the same with him, and making him known, made man, as the ray the sun.

73_marg1172: Upholding all things, etc. It was said above that through him he made all things. Here he now attributes to him the highest authority, because with authority he governs and contains all things. For as all things were created by him, so by him they are preserved unchanged. For the omnipotence of the Creator is the cause of the subsisting of every creature, and if this power should ever cease from ruling the things it has founded, the form and nature of all things would alike fall to ruin. And therefore the Lord says: “My Father worketh until now; and I work,” showing a certain continuation of the work of him who at once contains and administers all things. In this work his wisdom also perseveres, of which it is said: “She reacheth from end to end mightily, and ordereth all things sweetly.” God, therefore, almighty, in unchangeable eternity, will and truth, ever the same, moves the spiritual creature through time, and moves the bodily creature also through time and place, that by that motion he may minister to the natures which he has founded. When, therefore, he does anything of this kind, we ought not to suppose that his substance, by which he is God, is changeable in times and places, or moveable through times and places, since he is both within every thing, because in him are all things, and without every thing, because he is above all things; and older than all, because he is before all things; and newer than all, because the same himself is after all things, that is, after the beginnings of all things. And therefore, commending his power, the Apostle says: Upholding all things, etc. And note that it is said by way of likeness. For by saying this he wished to signify the ease of upholding, by a metaphor from those who without any labour move or effect something by a word or a finger; so Christ without labour contains and governs the mass and greatness of creation. Observe that although the Apostle here says that Christ contains all things, he said above that the Father made all things through him, where he says: “By whom also he made the world.” As though he could not himself make, unless the Father had stretched out his right hand to him, or as though he had been some instrument of the Father working. But if all things are governed by him, were they not made by him? So he was not, as you, heretic, vainly suppose, some instrument, nor is the Father said to have made through him as though he could not himself make. But as the Father is said to judge through the Son, because it is agreed that he begot him as maker. For if the Father is his cause according as he is Father, much more is he the cause of those things which are declared to have been made through the Son.

So the blessed Apostle does with the Hebrews, whom he raises little by little to the knowledge of God, mentioning lowly things among high ones, everywhere following the footsteps of his master. So in this whole series the Apostle first recalls high things, saying “in his Son,” where the Son is understood properly, who is higher and more excellent than all. Then he descends to lowly things, saying: “Whom he hath appointed heir.” Then he returns to high things, saying: “By whom also he made the world.” Afterwards he comes to a step higher than all, saying: Who being the brightness, etc. Then he speaks of lowly things: Making purgation of sins. In the first, candlesticks in the plural, because although it was one, it had seven branches. For in the middle was a shaft from which three branches proceeded on the right side and three on the left. The table, that is, the altar, after the entrance. And upon the table twelve loaves set before God, which were of fine flour, and every sabbath they were all changed. But if before the sabbath any were needed, it could not be taken unless another were at once put in its place. And upon the bread was shining frankincense. The first is called the holy places because of the veneration of that time, chiefly because it signified the present Church, which is holy. The second is called the holy of holies, because it was in greater veneration and because it signifies the “supercelestial Church,” where there is no sin. The ark was of setim wood, having two cubits and a half in length, and one and a half in breadth, as much in height. And at each corner a golden ring, two on the right and two on the left, in which golden bars were continually set for carrying. The propitiatory, or oracle, was a table over the ark of the same length and breadth. Over it stood the cherubim, and toward it, restraining themselves, they ever looked with faces turned toward each other. All this is a parable. The first tabernacle is the present Church, in which we fight for God before we come to heaven. In it the candlestick, that is, Christ shining in power and wisdom in the midst of the faithful, who are themselves golden candlesticks, because they shine with wisdom. Christ himself is the stem which bears three branches on the right and three on the left, because he is the vine on whom three orders are founded, which in the time of grace are on the right, that is, more worthy before grace, on the left. These are Noe, Daniel and Job, that is, rulers, the continent, the married. Who also, according to the gospel, are said to be in the field and in the bed and at the mill. The first part of the shafts was like golden reeds, then cups, then golden little spheres, lastly lilies. The reeds are the saints, who have been nourished in the waters of the divine fountain, and are hollow for pouring the liquid over to others. The cups themselves, while they give others to drink what they have drunk, namely the wisdom and knowledge of God. Then the little spheres, that is, round and perfect and mobile, whom nothing may hold back until they come to the lilies of eternal joy, who have neither the corner of fear nor the haughtiness of pride. Upon these were set seven lamps, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which remained most fully in Christ, and have been distributed to the faithful according to his will. The table at the door is divine Scripture, which remains, which is set before those who enter, which, while it shows the eternal joys and how they are reached, supplies the food of life. On it the clean loaves, that is, the twelve apostles and their successors, who offer to God the frankincense of prayers; if any of them dies, another must at once be put in his place. But in the seventh age all would be taken away. The second, after the veil, is the heavenly Church, which is veiled as long as we live here. The censer: Christ, full of the fire of charity, always making intercession for us. The ark: Christ, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” Golden on every side, because in his knowledge and speech and work there is nothing but pure truth. The length: perseverance of doctrine, which is signified by one cubit, and of operation, which is signified by the other cubit; for the perfection of which human understanding is imperfect, which the half cubit signifies. The breadth: perfection of charity; the height: perfection of hope, to which we are halves, that is, imperfect. The four rings: the four perfect evangelists, by whom he is carried into the four parts of the world. To which the golden bars always cling, that is, preachers shining with wisdom, always ready against enemies. In the ark an urn having manna, that is, the soul of Christ containing full wisdom, by which even the angels are refreshed. The rod signifies the “priestly power of Christ”; the tables, that he is the giver of the law; the propitiatory: Christ, who is propitiated to us; the two cherubim: all the orders of heaven which exist in him, who are joined together by love, and who, although wise, yet overshadow him as far as in them lies. 73_marg1398: The heifer, female: the weak flesh of Christ, red, bloody with the passion. They receive her from Moses, who is a figure of the law, because according to the law they thought they were slaying Christ, since according to them he broke the sabbath and profaned the legal observances. The heifer is without blemish, because the flesh of Christ is free from sins. And for confirmation he repeats, saying: “which hath no blemish in her.” Or for a distinction, namely that although in others who are his members it has blemish, yet in itself it has none. “And on which no yoke was laid,” because it is not subjected to iniquity; nay, finding men subjected, he freed them, and broke their bonds, and had power to lay down his life and to take it up again. It is said to be given not to Aaron but to Eleazar, because the Lord’s passion was to come not to the time that then was, but to the successors of that priesthood. It was cast out without the camp; so also the Lord was cast out without the city. And it was cast out into a clean place, because the Lord had no evil cause. It was slain in the sight of Eleazar; so the flesh of Christ was slain in the sight of those who were to be the priests of the Lord in the New Testament. Its blood he sprinkled over against the face of the testimony seven times, because Christ, according to the Scriptures, shed his blood for the remission of sins. Therefore over against the face of the testimony, because it was declared in no other way than it had been foretold by the divine testimony; therefore seven times, because that number pertains to spiritual cleanness. It was commanded to be burnt without the camp of Jerusalem. To be burnt, according to the Greeks, is named from suspension, because fire is moved upward and what is burnt is turned into it, which is a sign of the resurrection. It is said to be burnt in the sight of Eleazar, because the resurrection of Christ appeared to those who were to be a royal priesthood. Its skin is said to be burnt with the flesh and blood and dung, because not only the mortal substance of the body of Christ, which is signified by skin, flesh and blood, but also the insult and rejection of the people, which is signified by the name of dung, was turned into glory, which the flame of the burning signifies. The priest casts into the midst of the burning cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet. The cedar wood is hope, which dwells firmly in the heights. Hyssop: faith, which, though lowly, clings by its roots to the rock. Scarlet: charity, because by its fiery colour it bears witness to the fervour of the spirit. These three ought to be cast into the midst of the burning, that is, into the resurrection of Christ, that our life may be hid with him. The ashes, that is, the remains of the burning, are the fame that followed after the passion and resurrection. A clean man gathered this ash and laid it up in a clean place without the camp, because this fame was most famous among those who were not of the fellowship of the Jews, and were clean from the killing of Christ and outside the celebration of the Jewish custom. From this ash is made the water of sprinkling, by which baptism is signified, whence men were cleansed from contact with the dead, because from iniquity by the baptism of Christ. By that water proselytes as well as Gentiles, or Jews, were cleansed, because baptism profits Jews and Gentiles. That water was sprinkled with hyssop, which signifies faith, because hearts are cleansed by faith, and without faith baptism does not profit. This was done by a clean man, because the ministers of the Church, who bear the person of the Lord, ought to be truly clean.

73_marg1566: He refers the custom of the law to the mystery and the spiritual sense. The precept of the law was that on the tenth day of the seventh month after the paschal feast, namely on the feast of propitiation, they should take a calf and a goat and sacrifice them within the camp, and only the high priest would carry their blood into the holy of holies to pray for the people. But the flesh was to be burned outside the camp, and it was not lawful for anyone serving the tabernacle to eat of it. Christ, however, is that calf and goat; for he is the calf which the loving father sacrificed at the return of the prodigal son. He is also the goat which was offered for sinners. He is also the high priest who entered heaven, interceding for us. Within the camp of Jerusalem he was sacrificed by the voices and judgment of the Jews, but outside, on the cross, his flesh was burned by the fire of the passion. The altar where the flesh was burned outside the camp is the altar of the Church, where the body of the Lord is consecrated. Of this they have no power to eat who serve the body, that is, fornicators and drunkards and the like. As Christ, so also his own, outside the camp, that is, the conversation of seculars, being kindled by the Holy Spirit, consume whatever is carnal in them, mortifying themselves and putting to death their members with the vices and concupiscences. Or also by martyrdom their blood, that is, a life praiseworthy to God, is presented through Christ. Or blood, that is, their souls are borne into heaven. On the altar, that is, they are offered by faith. To which the carnal who love the world dare not approach. To fulfil which mystery Jesus suffered outside the gate.
